title: Die angeborenen Formen moeglicher Erfahrung
key_findings: Proposes the Kindchenschema (baby schema): large head relative to body, high forehead, large low-set eyes, round cheeks, short limbs, which releases caretaking/affection (as summarised by Glocker2009, Nittono2012, Borgi2014).
practical_applications: Origin of the cute-design levers used in chibi, kawaii, mascot and picture-book characters.
limitations: Not read; content known only via secondary sources. Ethological claim of innateness is debated.

title: Baby Schema in Infant Faces Induces Cuteness Perception and Motivation for Caretaking in Adults
authors: Melanie L. Glocker, Daniel D. Langleben, Kosha Ruparel, James W. Loughead, Ruben C. Gur, Norbert Sachser
key_findings: Parametric manipulation of real infant photos: high baby schema (round face, high forehead, big eyes, small nose/mouth) vs low (narrow face, low forehead).
n = 122 undergraduates: high-baby-schema infants rated cuter and elicited stronger caretaking motivation than unmanipulated and low versions.
Method (per Borgi2014): features adjusted within +/-2 SD of the natural range, so it does not test extreme cartoon exaggeration.
practical_applications: Quantified checklist for 'make it cuter': widen face, raise forehead, enlarge eyes, shrink nose and mouth.
limitations: Effects tested on photographic human infants inside natural range; generalisation to stylised cartoon proportions is inferred, not tested here.

title: Baby schema in human and animal faces induces cuteness perception and gaze allocation in children
authors: Marta Borgi, Irene Cogliati-Dezza, Victoria Brelsford, Kerstin Meints, Francesca Cirulli
key_findings: Six facial measures manipulated (face width, forehead length, eye width, nose length, nose width, mouth width) on human, dog and cat faces, following Glocker's method.
Children aged 3-6 (eye tracking, n = 50) looked longer at high-baby-schema faces across species; children (n = 32) and adults (n = 58) rated them cuter.
Eyes drew most fixations, then nose and mouth; children looked longer at the eye region of high-infantile faces.
practical_applications: Baby schema works on animal characters and on child audiences, not only adults; the eyes are the main lever.
limitations: Gaze effect near significance, driven by adult faces; photographic stimuli.

title: The Power of Kawaii: Viewing Cute Images Promotes a Careful Behavior and Narrows Attentional Focus
authors: Hiroshi Nittono, Michiko Fukushima, Akihiro Yano, Hiroki Moriya
key_findings: After viewing baby-animal images, fine-motor performance improved 43.9% vs 11.9% after adult animals (n = 48); visual search accuracy +15.7% vs +1.4% (adult) and +1.2% (pleasant food).
Global-precedence effect disappeared after cute images: attention narrowed to detail.
Pleasantness alone (food) did not produce the effect.
practical_applications: Cute characters can make viewers look closer and more carefully - useful before a detail-heavy panel or product close-up (DERIVED).
limitations: Small samples; Japanese university students; photographic animals, not drawn characters; replication not checked in this batch.

title: The two-layer model of 'kawaii': A behavioural science framework for understanding kawaii and cuteness
key_findings: Splits kawaii into two layers: an emotion and a social value.
The emotion is a positive feeling tied to social motivation to stay close to appealing people/objects; most typical toward infants but not limited to them.
Argues the biological trait is not culture-specific, but Japanese culture has cultivated it.
practical_applications: Kawaii design need not rely only on baby proportions: approachability and closeness are the target feeling.
limitations: Only the abstract was read; survey details not checked.

title: The evolution of the teddy bear
authors: R. A. Hinde, L. A. Barden
key_findings: (Per search summary of the paper and citing works) Museum teddy bears from 1903 onward show a trend toward a larger forehead and shorter snout; interpreted as selection by human preference for baby features.
(Per citing work Morris, Reddy & Bunting 1995) 6- and 8-year-olds preferred baby-featured bears; 4-year-olds did not.
practical_applications: Commercial characters drift toward baby schema over time - a known pattern for mascots and toys.
limitations: Not read directly; small museum sample; correlational.

title: Identification and ratings of caricatures: Implications for mental representations of faces
authors: Gillian Rhodes, Susan E. Brennan, Susan Carey
key_findings: Computer line-drawing caricatures (exaggerating all metric differences from a norm face) of familiar faces were identified faster than veridical drawings, which were faster than anticaricatures; accuracy did not differ.
The best likeness was judged to be a caricature (about +16% by interpolation, as reported by Frowd2007).
Supports norm-based (distance-from-average) face coding.
practical_applications: Exaggerate what makes a character differ from the average face; pulling a design toward 'average' makes it slower to recognise.
limitations: Familiar real faces as line drawings; does not test invented cartoon characters.

title: An application of caricature: how to improve the recognition of facial composites
authors: Charlie Frowd, Vicki Bruce, David Ross, Alex McIntyre, Peter J. B. Hancock
key_findings: Review section: best-likeness caricature level ~16% (Rhodes 1987) to ~42% (Benson & Perrett 1994) for line drawings, but only ~4-6% for photographs.
Caricatured line drawings are identified as well as or slightly better than veridical; anticaricatures less well.
For error-laden composites an anti-caricature was best - exaggeration also amplifies errors.
practical_applications: Stylised/line work tolerates far more exaggeration than photoreal rendering; exaggerate only features that are correct/distinctive.
limitations: Forensic composite context; effects for invented characters inferred.

title: A Study of Facial Features of American and Japanese Cartoon Characters
authors: Kun Liu, Junhong Chen, Kang-Ming Chang
key_findings: 100 American and Japanese animation characters measured against real faces (angles, lengths, areas).
Both traditions exaggerate eyes, nose, ears, forehead and chin.
Eye area: American characters ~2x human, Japanese characters ~3.4x human.
practical_applications: Starting numbers for eye scale per style: Western TV/feature ~2x, anime/manga ~3.4x real eye area.
limitations: Abstract only; sample selection and per-style variance not checked; Symmetry is an open-access MDPI journal (moderate tier).

title: The assessment of the biological age of children's characters created in the convention of Japanese animation in forensic practice
key_findings: 173 frontal anime faces (ages 10-18): eye-related ratios decrease and lower-face ratios (pupil-to-mouth, pupil-to-chin) increase with the character's stated age.
Age readable within +/-2 years for 67% of males but only 35% of females - female characters are drawn more paedomorphic.
Square chins appear only in the 16-18 male group; round/triangular chins in younger boys.
practical_applications: In anime-style design, age is signalled by eye size vs lower-face length and chin shape - use these to make age readable.
limitations: Forensic purpose; anime only; assigned ages imprecise.

title: The vocabulary of manga: Visual morphology in dialects of Japanese Visual Language
key_findings: Catalogued 73 conventionalised graphic schemas in manga (e.g. nosebleed for arousal, nose bubble for sleep) across 20 shonen and shojo books.
Most schemas appear in both genres (shared Japanese Visual Language) but in different proportions - genres act as dialects.
practical_applications: Manga-style expression sheets should include symbolic emblems, not only facial anatomy; shonen and shojo share the vocabulary.
limitations: Abstract/publisher page only; frequencies per schema not read.

title: The Uncanny Valley (translated by K. F. MacDorman and N. Kageki; original 1970)
key_findings: Affinity rises with human likeness, then dips sharply near (but short of) full human likeness; movement amplifies peaks and valleys.
Examples: toy robot (first hill), realistic prosthetic hand (valley), bunraku puppet (high affinity from a distance).
Recommends designers aim for the first peak - moderate human likeness - rather than risk the valley.
practical_applications: Clearly stylised characters are the safe default; near-photoreal characters need flawless detail and motion.
limitations: Essay/hypothesis, not data; the curve shape itself is weakly supported (see Katsyri2015).

title: A review of empirical evidence on different uncanny valley hypotheses: support for perceptual mismatch as one road to the valley of eeriness
authors: Jari Katsyri, Klaus Forger, Meeri Makarainen, Tapio Takala
key_findings: Naive uncanny dip for any human-likeness increase: weak (1 of 8 studies); linear rise of affinity with human likeness: 7 of 9.
Inconsistent realism across features (e.g. realistic face with mismatched eyes, face-voice mismatch): strongest support (4 of 4).
Atypical features on humanlike faces (e.g. enlarged eyes on realistic faces): good support (3 of 4). Movement amplification: not supported.
practical_applications: Keep one realism level across eyes, skin, shape, motion and voice; never put anime-size eyes on photoreal skin.
limitations: Small, heterogeneous, mostly self-report evidence base; morphing artefacts may confound.

title: To Stylize or not to Stylize? The Effect of Shape and Material Stylization on the Perception of Computer-Generated Faces
authors: Eduard Zell, Carlos Aliaga, Adrian Jarabo, Katja Zibrek, Diego Gutierrez, Rachel McDonnell, Mario Botsch
key_findings: Shape stylization drives perceived realism and expression intensity (expressions read as more intense on more stylised shapes); material/texture drives appeal, reassurance and attractiveness.
Strong mismatch between shape and material stylization lowers appeal and raises eeriness (abstract shapes + realistic materials = highly eerie).
Realism is a poor predictor of appeal (appeal and realism scales do not correlate); blurring realistic skin texture raises appeal and lowers eeriness with little realism loss.
practical_applications: For AI images: if the shape is cartoon, keep the surface cartoon (flat/soft), and soften textures rather than adding pores.
limitations: 3D CG faces of two people; lab ratings; generalisation to 2D drawing inferred.

title: Render me Real? Investigating the Effect of Render Style on the Perception of Animated Virtual Humans
authors: Rachel McDonnell, Martin Breidt, Heinrich H. Bulthoff
key_findings: (Per search summaries/citing papers) Render style affects appeal and perceived realism of animated humans; animation artefacts were more acceptable on cartoon-rendered than realistic characters; highly realistic and highly abstract styles were treated differently from middle styles.
practical_applications: Cartoon rendering buys tolerance for imperfect motion - relevant to cheap rig/AI-video animation.
limitations: Not read; details unverified.

title: Iconic faces are not real faces: enhanced emotion detection and altered neural processing as faces become more iconic
authors: L. N. Kendall, Quentin Raffaelli, Alan Kingstone, Rebecca M. Todd
key_findings: Five stimulus sets from photorealistic to fully iconic: at brief presentation, emotion identification was more accurate for more cartoonised faces; at the fastest times the simplest images were ~60% more accurate than realistic faces.
Higher contrast and lower featural complexity each improved accuracy independently.
Simpler/higher-contrast faces produced lower P1 amplitudes (less early cortical processing needed).
practical_applications: For feeds and thumbnails, simplified high-contrast cartoon faces communicate emotion faster than realistic faces.
limitations: Lab task with brief exposures; small set of basic emotions.

title: Transfer between Picture Books and the Real World by Very Young Children
authors: Patricia A. Ganea, Megan Bloom Pickard, Judy S. DeLoache
key_findings: 15- and 18-month-olds extended new labels between pictures and real objects more often with photographs and realistic drawings than with cartoons; iconicity aids transfer.
practical_applications: For toddler educational content where real-world transfer matters, prefer realistic illustration over heavy cartoon stylisation.
limitations: Very young children only; effect shrinks with age (Strouse2018).

title: The Role of Book Features in Young Children's Transfer of Information from Picture Books to Real-World Contexts
authors: Gabrielle A. Strouse, Angela Nyhout, Patricia A. Ganea
key_findings: Realism: photos easiest, cartoons hardest for 15-18-month transfer; iconicity still matters at age 3 in some tasks.
Anthropomorphic language/illustrations reduced factual learning and increased attribution of human traits to real animals (Ganea et al. 2014).
Sharing story with human characters increased children's sharing; the same story with a raccoon decreased it (Larsen et al. 2017).
Manipulative features (flaps, pop-ups) reduced learning in toddlers (Tare et al. 2010).
practical_applications: Teach facts or behaviours with human (or realistic) characters; keep talking-animal designs for entertainment/brand warmth.
limitations: Few studies per domain; small samples; mostly Western urban children.

title: Color Psychology: Effects of Perceiving Color on Psychological Functioning in Humans
authors: Andrew J. Elliot, Markus A. Maier
key_findings: Colour can carry meaning and affect affect, cognition and behaviour, but the literature is nascent; boundary conditions and real-world generalisability are needed before strong application recommendations.
practical_applications: Treat character colour-personality coding as craft convention, not science.
limitations: Abstract only; not specific to characters.

title: The Illusion of Life: Disney Animation
key_findings: Source of the 12 principles incl. 'appeal', 'exaggeration' and 'solid drawing' (as summarised in CHARACTER_DESIGN.md and SHAPE_LANGUAGE.md).
practical_applications: Vocabulary for appeal, exaggeration, twinning avoidance.
limitations: Not read this session; practitioner (craft) knowledge.

title: Understanding Comics: The Invisible Art
key_findings: Proposes 'amplification through simplification': simplified iconic faces invite reader identification (theory cited as motivation by Kendall2016, which tested a related claim).
practical_applications: Rationale for simple faces on protagonists + more detailed environments.
limitations: Not read this session; theory, partly supported by Kendall2016 for emotion speed only.

title: Model Sheets for Character Designers (Clip Studio guide)
key_findings: A model sheet set = construction sheet (proportions in heads), head + body turnaround, colour sheet, expression sheet, pose sheet.
Turnaround minimum: front, back, profile, three-quarter; horizontal guide lines for eye centres, brows, chin, shoulders keep views aligned.
Expression sheet: at least joy, sadness, anger, surprise; ~6 samples; pose sheet 4-5 poses.
practical_applications: Template for the turnaround/model-sheet section and AI master images.
limitations: Single practitioner; numbers are recommendations, not standards.

title: Early studio animation before rubber hose (animationstudies 2.0 blog)
key_findings: Pre-1928 studio style (from Bray, 1914) had single brisk speed, little squash/stretch, animation on 4s, cycles; rubber hose era marked by rubberised limbs and synchronised sound from 1928.
practical_applications: Context for rubber hose spec card: fluid limbs paired with music timing.
limitations: Blog by an animation scholar; brief.

title: Rubber hose animation
key_findings: Limbs drawn as flowing unjointed curves; rounder smoother bodies (Bill Nolan, Felix shorts, 1920s); style suited sound/music sync; declined in the 1930s with the move to anatomical realism; revived in later TV and games.
practical_applications: Spec card for rubber-hose style.
limitations: Community source; gloves/pie-eyes traits not covered and so not asserted.

title: Chibi (style)
key_findings: Super deformed: head roughly 1/3 to 1/2 of total height vs ~7-8 heads for a typical anime character; oversized head and eyes, tiny nose, stubby limbs, details dropped, signature hair/accessory emphasised; widely used in merchandise and for exaggerated reactions.
practical_applications: Spec card for chibi/SD.
limitations: Community source; proportions are convention.

title: Character Design and Visual Development for LINE Stickers: 'Yoga Teacher'
key_findings: Thai LINE sticker character built with persona research + silhouette-first design + Super Deformed proportion + split-complementary bright colours with grey/white; large face for clear emotion.
40 stickers; 30 target users: 93.3% understood the messages, 90.0% satisfied, 96.7% felt it could represent them.
practical_applications: Workflow for Thai sticker/mascot characters: persona -> silhouette -> SD proportion -> palette -> expression set with short Thai phrases.
limitations: Practice-based design research; satisfaction survey without control.

title: Brand Communication by Using Spoke-characters Featured in LINE Stickers in Thailand
key_findings: Content analysis of 5 popular 2018 sponsored LINE sticker sets: characters created specifically for stickers, usually more than one per brand, mostly gender-unidentifiable, all humorous.
Focus groups (n = 18): a duck character linked to a restaurant's roast-duck dish built brand association; characters with no link to the brand did not.
Users favour cute, funny, often animal characters behaving like everyday life (as reported).
practical_applications: A brand character must carry a visible link to the product/service; casts of 2+ characters are the norm in Thai brand stickers.
limitations: Small sample; one year; qualitative.

title: Thai Comics in the Twenty-First Century: Identity and Diversity of a New Generation of Thai Cartoonists (research project)
key_findings: Early Thai long-story comics (1930s) were stylistically inspired by American newspaper/animation cartoon strips; a realistic illustrative style was introduced by Hem Vejakorn (1938) via Siamese-Italian academic painting.

Kai Hua Roh (gag magazine, 1973, slogan 'household humour') and Maha Sanook (1976, younger readers, short comic stories) from Banlue; pocket format; one-baht comics with simple moral plots peaked in the late 1970s-80s.

Mainstream Thai comics of the 1990s-2000s were strongly manga-influenced; the 21st-century independent generation shows 'freedom of style' (European, American and Japanese influences); individual gag cartoonists' styles vary widely (one is compared with loose European illustrators).
practical_applications: Thai cartoon tradition = plural, not one look; when prompting 'Thai gag comic' describe concrete traits (format, line, humour) rather than a single house style.
limitations: Academic research report; no systematic analysis of proportions or line in Kai Hua Roh.

title: Khan Kluay (2006 film)
key_findings: First Thai 3D animated feature (Kantana Animation, 2006), directed by a former Disney/Blue Sky animator; title character a brave blue elephant who becomes a royal war elephant; budget 115 M baht, 3-year production; multiple Thai and international awards.
practical_applications: Reference point for Thai CG feature style: stylised animals in a historical Thai setting with non-natural signature colour.
limitations: Encyclopedia; no design analysis available.

title: From Webtoon to Apptoon: Changes of Korean Webtoon's Displaying code
key_findings: First-generation webtoons used vertical layout for mouse scrolling with extended panels and creative gutters; app versions shrink frames to phone size and use zoom/pan/vertical movement transitions as directing grammar.
practical_applications: Webtoon characters must read in small, tightly framed panels viewed one at a time while scrolling.
limitations: Short essay; does not discuss character drawing directly.
